title: Super Intelligence-Era Critical Infrastructure Cyber Defense Plan | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: Former Deputy NSA Anne Neuberger argues AI is collapsing the time from vulnerability discovery to exploitation, and proposes a CEO-led, ISAC-delivered plan under the White House's Super Intelligence Force to contain exposure at the few hundred US power, payments, water, telecom and hospital operators and shared vendors whose failure would cascade nationally. The plan prioritizes containment within 6 months (no internet-exposed control systems, segmentation, 72-hour manual operation), AI-driven flaw discovery and workarounds tested on digital twins, and legal fixes such as CISA 2015 reauthorization and safe harbors.

insights.claim: AI is shrinking the time between when a vulnerability is discovered and when it is exploited, so cyber defenders operating at human speed will lose the race.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Demand shifts toward machine-speed, AI-native defense tooling; human-speed SOC/patch workflows become structurally obsolete.
insights.quote: Defenders who still work at human speed will lose that race.
insights.locator: AI is shrinking the time between

insights.claim: The same AI that accelerates attackers can serve defenders by finding exposed systems, ranking which matter most, and generating fixes or workarounds such as firewall rules or settings changes for unpatchable legacy equipment; the open question is speed of application.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: AI-driven exposure management, prioritization and auto-remediation are positioned as the core defensive category.
insights.quote: The question is whether it can be applied fast enough.

insights.claim: Operational technology that runs physical infrastructure often stays in service for more than 20 years and some of it cannot be patched without risking outages, making patch-centric defense incompatible with AI-speed exploitation.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Compensating-control, segmentation and OT-security vendors benefit over pure patch-management players.
insights.quote: Operational technology (OT, the systems that run physical equipment) often stays in service for more than 20 years.
insights.locator: The threat and the regulatory gap

insights.claim: Current cyber regulation is mismatched to AI-era threats because it relies on fixed patch windows and a compliance mindset that checks whether controls exist rather than measuring exposure and containment speed.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Watch for regulators moving to outcomes-based metrics, which would reshape compliance-software and audit spend.
insights.locator: Current regulatory rules were not built

themes.theme: Concentrated systemic risk: the critical few hundred

insights.claim: National cyber risk to US critical infrastructure is concentrated: cascading failures run through only a few hundred operators and their shared vendors, so protecting those first buys time to fix the rest, while smaller operators remain soft entry points.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Security budgets and policy attention will concentrate on a narrow set of systemically important operators and their vendors.
insights.quote: The most significant national risk is concentrated, fortunately.

insights.claim: Operators should be ranked by how much harm their failure causes and how many others depend on them rather than by size, and shared vendors often carry more risk than any single operator.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Shared vendors (cloud, core-banking, EHR) face rising scrutiny and mandated security obligations.
insights.quote: Shared vendors often carry more risk than any single operator.

insights.claim: The plan's priority targets across five sectors are: power (large transmission substations, balancing authorities, black-start plants), payments (Fedwire, ACH, CHIPS, clearing houses, shared cloud and core-banking vendors), water utilities serving 50,000+ people (especially chemical dosing controls), telecom (internet routing, core mobile network, 911, timing signals), and hospitals (regional trauma centers, EHR vendors, medical device makers).
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Defines the target customer map for critical-infrastructure security vendors.

insights.claim: Every sector depends on power and telecom, and every sector runs on the major cloud providers (Microsoft, AWS, Google) and increasingly frontier AI labs, which the plan would make SI Force CEO Council members responsible for AI defense tools and vendor flaw discovery.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Hyperscalers and frontier labs gain a formal national-defense role, potentially deepening government relationships and contracts.

insights.claim: Neuberger proposes a public-private governance model where the White House's Super Intelligence Force sets national targets, critical-infrastructure CEOs commit their sectors to them, and Sector Coordinating Councils and ISACs deliver and measure the work.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Signals a policy channel through which industry-specific AI security procurement could be coordinated at sector level.

insights.claim: Today only the power and financial services ISACs have CEO-level involvement, while the water, telecom and hospital ISACs do not, so the SI Force would need to push influential CEOs to create CEO layers in those sectors.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Water, telecom and hospitals are the laggard sectors where governance and spending upgrades would be largest.
insights.quote: Today, the power and financial services sector ISACs have CEO-level involvement; the water, telecom and hospital ISACs do not.
insights.locator: The U.S. has a governance system

insights.claim: Accountability would come from CEOs signing sector targets (zero internet-exposed control systems, passed 72-hour manual-operation drills, critical vulnerabilities contained within a set time), monthly anonymized ISAC scorecards to the SI Force, and CEO-level reviews for sectors behind target.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Creates measurable KPIs that would drive demand for exposure scanning, segmentation and resilience testing products.

insights.claim: Public-company boards would attest to outcomes-based progress metrics consistent with SEC cyber disclosure rules, and regulators would accept that attestation instead of duplicate audits as an incentive to participate.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Could reduce audit/compliance duplication costs while raising board-level cyber liability.

insights.claim: Large operators would sponsor small ones: utilities for co-ops and city utilities, large health systems for rural hospitals, big banks funding community-bank tools through FS-ISAC, and national carriers backstopping rural carriers.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Shifts security costs onto large incumbents; watch for sponsored security programs as a sales channel.

insights.claim: Within 3-6 months the CEO council would run a cross-sector drill modeled on GridEx in which power, telecom, banks and hospitals respond together to an AI-speed attack.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: A near-term catalyst to watch for evidence the plan is being adopted.

insights.claim: ISACs would evolve from CISO-level threat-alert sharing into sector work drivers providing shared AI detection and exposure-scanning tools, a single coordinated channel to vendors for AI-discovered flaws, mutual aid building on Cyber Mutual Assistance and Sheltered Harbor, and a single scorecard so companies report once.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: ISACs could become meaningful aggregated buyers or distributors of AI security tooling.

themes.theme: Technical playbook: contain, prove resilience, scale with AI

insights.claim: The technical strategy prioritizes containment over replacement: eliminate internet exposure of control systems, use one-way data diodes for the most critical networks, separate IT from control networks and segment by site, and keep offline configuration backups with bare-metal rebuild capability.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Favors OT segmentation, data-diode, secure remote access and phishing-resistant MFA vendors.

insights.claim: Every top target should prove it can operate without its IT systems for 72 hours in drills, with hospitals using paper charts, utilities manual control, and banks fallback settlement.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: A concrete resilience standard that would drive spending on drills, fallback processes and recovery tooling.

insights.claim: AI vulnerability discovery would be run on open source, vendor code and firmware before release, with findings sent through a national clearinghouse and vendors required to provide a fix or workaround on a set timeline that gives critical infrastructure a head start before broad distribution.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: AI-based code and firmware scanning becomes a mandated workflow; beneficiaries include AI labs and vuln-discovery startups.

insights.claim: AI labs should work with industrial control system makers to build digital twins of standard equipment so AI-generated fixes and workarounds can be tested before touching live grids or water plants, and the administration's Gold Eagle AI vulnerability clearinghouse should expand from software into industrial equipment.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Digital-twin and OT simulation platforms gain a security use case; watch Gold Eagle's scope expansion.
insights.locator: In addition to the existing ISACs

insights.claim: CDNs, firewall providers, telcos and cloud networking firms like Cloudflare could block or redirect malicious traffic at national scale before it reaches operational systems, but this may require government authorities and legal liability protections.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Network-edge providers could gain a quasi-public defense role; liability legislation is the gating factor.

insights.claim: Small water systems, rural hospitals and electric co-ops that cannot afford security staff would get a subsidized AI security operations service, with nonprofit funding already available.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Opens a subsidized SMB critical-infrastructure market for AI-SOC providers.
insights.locator: Monitor for operators who can’t afford staff

insights.claim: As a guardrail, AI defense tools should be read-only on control networks by default, with a human approving any change.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Sets a design constraint for OT-facing AI security products: human-in-the-loop, read-only by default.
insights.quote: AI defense tools are read-only for control networks by default, and a human approves any change.

insights.claim: CEOs will not authorize sensitive data sharing without legal cover and firms may be liable for vulnerabilities they identify, so the plan calls for long-term reauthorization of the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 and some form of time-based liability protection.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: CISA 2015 reauthorization and liability safe-harbor legislation are key policy catalysts to track.
insights.quote: CEOs will not authorize sensitive data sharing without legal cover

insights.claim: Companies meeting outcomes-based targets with board sign-off would receive safe harbor protections, and regulators would track zero exposed control systems, time to contain critical flaws, and proven hours of manual operation instead of checklists.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: A shift from checklist compliance to outcomes metrics could disrupt GRC/compliance vendors and reward telemetry-based measurement.

insights.claim: Vendors, many of them foreign equipment makers, would have to act on AI-discovered flaws by a deadline as a condition of selling to critical operators, disclose product support lifetimes, and meet secure-by-default federal purchasing requirements.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Foreign ICS/OT vendors face market-access risk; domestic secure-by-default suppliers could gain share.
insights.quote: Equipment makers, many of them foreign, should have to act on findings by a deadline as a condition for selling to critical operators.
insights.locator: In addition to the existing ISACs

insights.claim: The federal government would secure frontier-model access and compute for participating companies and the national vulnerability clearinghouse, and build a surge reserve of vetted responders drawn from large operators and vendors.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Government becomes a buyer of frontier-model access and compute for defense, a tailwind for AI labs and cloud providers.

insights.claim: Top targets should be contained within 6 months because replacing unsupported equipment is costly and takes 2-5 years; addressing national tech debt will be expensive and should be prioritized for systemically critical operators that cannot afford upgrades alone.
insights.speaker: Anne Neuberger
insights.so_what: Near-term spend goes to containment; longer-term equipment replacement cycle (2-5 years) is a later, larger opportunity.
insights.quote: Some have proposed replacing unsupported equipment but that is costly and can take 2–5 years, which is why containment comes first.
